chunks.title: EC2 instance unreachable
chunks.text: SSH or HTTP connections to an EC2 instance time out, although the console shows the instance as running.

chunks.title: EC2 instance unreachable
chunks.text: Check the instance status checks: a failed system check points at AWS hardware, a failed instance check points at the operating system, such as a full disk or a broken fstab. Verify the security group allows the port from your IP, the network ACL allows both inbound traffic and the outbound ephemeral port range, and the subnet route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. Confirm the instance has a public IP or Elastic IP. Use the EC2 serial console or "Get system log" to read boot messages.

chunks.title: EC2 instance unreachable
chunks.text: Add the missing security group or NACL rule, attach an Elastic IP, or fix the route table. For a failed system check, stop and start the instance to move it to new hardware. For an operating system problem, detach the root volume, attach it to a rescue instance and repair it.

chunks.title: EC2 instance unreachable
chunks.text: Manage network rules with infrastructure as code, enable CloudWatch alarms with automatic recovery on status check failure, and use Session Manager so access does not depend on open inbound ports.

chunks.title: AWS Lambda function timing out
chunks.text: Invocations end with "Task timed out after 3.00 seconds", API Gateway returns 504 or 503, and CloudWatch shows durations equal to the configured timeout.

chunks.title: AWS Lambda function timing out
chunks.text: Read the CloudWatch log stream for the REPORT line, which gives duration, billed duration, memory used and init duration. A long init duration indicates slow cold starts from heavy imports. A Lambda attached to a VPC has no internet access unless its private subnets route through a NAT gateway, so calls to public APIs hang until the timeout. Downstream calls without client timeouts also consume the whole budget.

chunks.title: AWS Lambda function timing out
chunks.text: Increase the timeout and memory; more memory also allocates more CPU. Set explicit connect and read timeouts on HTTP and database clients. Use VPC endpoints for AWS services such as S3 and DynamoDB instead of a NAT gateway. Move heavy initialisation outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it. API Gateway has a 29 second integration limit, so long work should be moved to an asynchronous queue.

chunks.title: AWS Lambda function timing out
chunks.text: Alarm on duration approaching the timeout and on error rate, enable X-Ray tracing to see slow dependencies, and keep deployment packages small.

chunks.title: S3 returns AccessDenied
chunks.text: `aws s3 cp` or an SDK call fails with "An error occurred (AccessDenied)" or HTTP 403, while other principals can read the same bucket.

chunks.title: S3 returns AccessDenied
chunks.text: Identify the caller with `aws sts get-caller-identity`. Access requires an allow in the IAM identity policy and no explicit deny in the bucket policy, a service control policy or a VPC endpoint policy. Objects encrypted with a customer managed KMS key also require kms:Decrypt on that key. For cross-account uploads, Object Ownership settings determine who owns the object. Use the IAM policy simulator and CloudTrail events to find the denying statement.

chunks.title: S3 returns AccessDenied
chunks.text: Grant the missing s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject or s3:ListBucket action on the correct ARN; note that ListBucket applies to the bucket ARN and object actions apply to `bucket/*`. Add kms:Decrypt for encrypted objects. Remove or scope explicit deny statements. Keep Block Public Access enabled and share data through presigned URLs rather than public ACLs.

chunks.title: S3 returns AccessDenied
chunks.text: Define bucket and IAM policies in infrastructure as code, use IAM Access Analyzer to review access, and grant least-privilege roles per workload.

chunks.title: Cron job does not run
chunks.text: A scheduled script works when run by hand but produces no output or side effects when started by cron.

chunks.title: Cron job does not run
chunks.text: Confirm cron started the job with `grep CRON /var/log/syslog` or `journalctl -u cron`. Cron runs with a minimal environment: PATH is usually only /usr/bin:/bin, the working directory is the home directory and no shell profile is loaded. Errors are mailed to the user and silently lost when no mail transfer agent is installed. A crontab line without a trailing newline, or a `%` character that is not escaped, also breaks the entry.

chunks.title: Cron job does not run
chunks.text: Use absolute paths for commands and files, set PATH at the top of the crontab, and redirect output with `>> /var/log/job.log 2>&1` so failures are visible. Escape `%` as `\%`. Make the script executable and give it a shebang line.

chunks.title: Cron job does not run
chunks.text: Consider systemd timers, which log to the journal and support `Persistent=true` to catch up on missed runs, and add a heartbeat check that alerts when a job has not completed on schedule.

chunks.title: Root filesystem is full
chunks.text: Writes fail with "No space left on device". Services crash while writing logs or temporary files, package installs abort, and `df -h /` reports 100% use on the root filesystem.

chunks.title: Root filesystem is full
chunks.text: Run `df -h` to confirm which mount is full, then `sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h` to find the largest top-level directories without crossing into other mounts. The usual culprits are /var/log, /var/lib/docker, /tmp and core dumps. Check the systemd journal size with `journalctl --disk-usage`. A file that was deleted while a process still holds it open keeps consuming space; list those with `sudo lsof +L1`.

chunks.title: Root filesystem is full
chunks.text: Vacuum the journal with `sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M`. Compress or remove rotated logs under /var/log. Clean the package cache with `sudo apt-get clean` or `sudo dnf clean all`. For deleted-but-open files, restart the owning service so the kernel releases the blocks. Remove old kernels with `sudo apt-get autoremove`.

chunks.title: Root filesystem is full
chunks.text: Set `SystemMaxUse=` in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, configure logrotate with compression and a retention count, and alert when disk usage crosses 80%. Keep application data on a separate volume so a runaway log cannot fill the root filesystem.

chunks.title: DNS resolution failures
chunks.text: Commands fail with "Temporary failure in name resolution" or "Could not resolve host", while connecting by IP address still works.

chunks.title: DNS resolution failures
chunks.text: Check which resolver is configured in /etc/resolv.conf; on systemd-resolved hosts it points to 127.0.0.53 and `resolvectl status` shows the upstream servers. Query directly with `dig example.com @1.1.1.1` to separate resolver problems from network problems. Confirm outbound UDP and TCP port 53 are allowed by the firewall. Inside Docker, containers copy the host resolver configuration at start-up.

chunks.title: DNS resolution failures
chunks.text: Restart the resolver with `sudo systemctl restart systemd-resolved`, correct the upstream servers in the netplan or NetworkManager configuration, or point resolv.conf at a working resolver. In a VPC, make sure DNS resolution and DNS hostnames are enabled. Restart containers after fixing the host resolver.

chunks.title: DNS resolution failures
chunks.text: Configure at least two resolvers, monitor resolution latency from each host, and avoid hand-editing resolv.conf on systems where a network manager regenerates it.

chunks.title: Docker consuming all disk space
chunks.text: /var/lib/docker grows until the host runs out of space, image pulls fail, and builds stop with "no space left on device".

chunks.title: Docker consuming all disk space
chunks.text: Run `docker system df -v` to break usage down into images, containers, local volumes and build cache. Dangling images from repeated builds, stopped containers, unused volumes and an unbounded BuildKit cache are the usual causes. Large container log files live under /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log.

chunks.title: Docker consuming all disk space
chunks.text: Remove unused objects with `docker system prune`; add `-a` to remove all images not used by a container and `--volumes` only after confirming no volume holds data you need. Clear the build cache with `docker builder prune --keep-storage 5GB`. Truncate an oversized container log with `truncate -s 0` on the JSON log file.

chunks.title: Docker consuming all disk space
chunks.text: Configure log rotation in /etc/docker/daemon.json with `"log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}`, schedule a weekly prune with a systemd timer, and keep /var/lib/docker on its own volume.

chunks.title: Container stuck in a restart loop
chunks.text: `docker ps` shows a container with status "Restarting" or an uptime that never exceeds a few seconds, and the service is intermittently unavailable.

chunks.title: Container stuck in a restart loop
chunks.text: Read the output of the last attempt with `docker logs --tail 100 container`. Inspect the exit code with `docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' container`. Exit code 137 means the process was killed, usually by the OOM killer; 1 is an application error; 126 and 127 mean the entrypoint is not executable or not found. A failing HEALTHCHECK combined with an orchestrator restart policy produces the same pattern.

chunks.title: Container stuck in a restart loop
chunks.text: Fix the configuration error reported in the logs, such as a missing environment variable or an unreachable database. Raise the memory limit if OOMKilled is true. Run the image interactively with `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh image` to debug the entrypoint. Temporarily set `--restart no` to stop the loop while investigating.

chunks.title: Container stuck in a restart loop
chunks.text: Validate configuration at start-up with clear error messages, add backoff when waiting for dependencies, and test images in CI with a smoke test that calls the health endpoint.

chunks.title: Sustained high CPU load
chunks.text: The server feels slow, requests time out and the load average reported by `uptime` stays well above the number of CPU cores for minutes at a time.

chunks.title: Sustained high CPU load
chunks.text: Use `top` or `htop` sorted by CPU to find the busiest processes. Load average counts runnable and uninterruptible tasks, so a high load with idle CPUs points at processes blocked on disk or network I/O; check the `wa` column in `top` and run `iostat -x 1`. Use `pidstat -u 1` to see per-process usage over time and `perf top` to see hot functions. On virtual machines a high `st` (steal) value means the hypervisor is starving the guest.

chunks.title: Sustained high CPU load
chunks.text: Restart or throttle the runaway process, lower its priority with `renice +10 -p PID`, or cap it with a systemd `CPUQuota=` setting. If steal time is high, move to a larger or non-burstable instance type. Fix the root cause in code, such as busy loops, missing caching or unbounded retries.

chunks.title: Sustained high CPU load
chunks.text: Track CPU, load average and steal time per host, set CPU limits on containers and systemd units, and load-test before releases so regressions are caught early.

chunks.title: Inodes exhausted while disk space remains
chunks.text: New files cannot be created and the error is "No space left on device", yet `df -h` still shows free gigabytes. Mail queues, PHP session directories and cache folders stop accepting new entries.

chunks.title: Inodes exhausted while disk space remains
chunks.text: Run `df -i` and look for a mount at or near 100% IUse. Find the directory holding millions of small files with `sudo find / -xdev -type f | cut -d/ -f2-3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -n | tail`. Common sources are session files, cache shards, unprocessed mail and orphaned build artefacts.

chunks.title: Inodes exhausted while disk space remains
chunks.text: Delete the small files in bulk with `find /path -type f -mtime +7 -delete`, which is far faster than `rm *` and avoids "argument list too long". If the directory belongs to an application, stop the application first. Inode counts on ext4 are fixed at format time, so a filesystem that legitimately needs more inodes must be recreated with `mkfs.ext4 -N` or migrated to XFS, which allocates inodes dynamically.

chunks.title: Inodes exhausted while disk space remains
chunks.text: Monitor inode usage alongside byte usage, add cleanup timers for session and cache directories, and store large numbers of tiny objects in a database or object store instead of the filesystem.

chunks.title: Free memory looks low because of page cache
chunks.text: Monitoring shows almost no free memory on a healthy server, and `free -h` reports a small "free" value while applications run normally.

chunks.title: Free memory looks low because of page cache
chunks.text: Read the "available" column in `free -h`, not "free". Linux uses otherwise idle RAM for the page cache to speed up file access, and that cache is released immediately when applications need memory. Real memory pressure shows up as a low available value, swap activity in `vmstat 1` (si and so columns), or OOM killer events.

chunks.title: Free memory looks low because of page cache
chunks.text: No action is needed when available memory is healthy. Do not routinely run `echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches`, which only discards useful cache and slows the system. If available memory is genuinely low, find the largest consumers with `ps aux --sort=-rss` and reduce their usage or add RAM.

chunks.title: Free memory looks low because of page cache
chunks.text: Alert on available memory and swap-in rate rather than free memory, and document the difference for anyone reading dashboards.

chunks.title: Intermittent network packet loss
chunks.text: Connections stall or reset intermittently, throughput is far below the link speed, and latency to some destinations spikes while others are fine.

chunks.title: Intermittent network packet loss
chunks.text: Run `mtr -rwzc 100 destination` to see loss and latency per hop; loss that starts at one hop and continues to the destination is real, while loss only at intermediate hops is often ICMP rate limiting. Check interface errors and drops with `ip -s link` and `ethtool -S eth0`. Test for MTU problems with `ping -M do -s 1472 destination`; failures at that size behind a VPN or tunnel indicate a path MTU issue.

chunks.title: Intermittent network packet loss
chunks.text: Replace faulty cables or move to a healthy interface when error counters grow. Lower the MTU or enable TCP MSS clamping on tunnels. Raise NIC ring buffers with `ethtool -G` if drops are caused by bursts. Escalate to the provider with mtr output when loss starts outside your network.

chunks.title: Intermittent network packet loss
chunks.text: Monitor interface error counters, latency and loss with continuous probes, and record MTU settings for every tunnel and VPN.

chunks.title: nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway
chunks.text: Users see "502 Bad Gateway" from nginx while nginx itself is running. The error log shows "connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream" or "upstream prematurely closed connection".

chunks.title: nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway
chunks.text: Read /var/log/nginx/error.log for the exact upstream error. Confirm the backend process (gunicorn, uvicorn, php-fpm, Node) is running and listening on the address in `proxy_pass` with `ss -ltnp`. For Unix sockets, check that the socket file exists and that the nginx worker user can read it. Test the backend directly with `curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health`.

chunks.title: nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway
chunks.text: Start or restart the backend service, fix a mismatched port or socket path, and correct socket permissions. If workers crash under load, increase their count or memory. When responses are slow rather than refused, raise `proxy_read_timeout`, though a 504 Gateway Timeout is the more typical symptom of slowness.

chunks.title: nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway
chunks.text: Run backends under systemd with restart policies, add a health check endpoint, and alert on the rate of 5xx responses in the nginx access log.

chunks.title: Process killed by the OOM killer
chunks.text: A process disappears without an application error, a container exits with code 137, or a service restarts unexpectedly. Kernel logs contain "Out of memory: Killed process".

chunks.title: Process killed by the OOM killer
chunks.text: Search the kernel ring buffer with `dmesg -T | grep -i -E "killed process|out of memory"` or `journalctl -k`. The log lists the victim, its resident memory and the cgroup that hit its limit. Compare against the memory limit of the container or systemd unit (`systemctl show -p MemoryMax unit`). Use `free -h` and `ps aux --sort=-rss | head` to see current consumers.

chunks.title: Process killed by the OOM killer
chunks.text: Raise the memory limit if the workload legitimately needs more, or reduce memory use by lowering worker counts, heap sizes or batch sizes. For a JVM, set `-Xmx` below the container limit. Add a modest swap file to absorb short spikes on small instances. Protect critical daemons by setting `OOMScoreAdjust=-500` in their unit files.

chunks.title: Process killed by the OOM killer
chunks.text: Alert on memory usage approaching limits, set explicit requests and limits for every container, and profile memory growth to catch leaks before they reach production.

chunks.title: Port already in use
chunks.text: A service fails to start with "bind: address already in use" or "EADDRINUSE", or Docker reports "port is already allocated".

chunks.title: Port already in use
chunks.text: Find the listener with `sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :8080'` or `sudo lsof -i :8080`. The holder is often an earlier instance of the same service, a container that publishes the port, or a socket-activated systemd unit. Sockets in TIME_WAIT do not block a new listener when the application sets SO_REUSEADDR.

chunks.title: Port already in use
chunks.text: Stop the conflicting process or container, or move one of the services to a different port. If an old instance did not exit, check why its shutdown hangs and kill it with `kill -TERM PID`, escalating to `kill -9` only if needed. For a socket-activated unit, stop both the .socket and the .service units.

chunks.title: Port already in use
chunks.text: Document port assignments per host, manage services through systemd or Compose so duplicate instances are not started by hand, and make applications read the port from configuration.

chunks.title: PostgreSQL "too many clients already"
chunks.text: Applications fail with "FATAL: sorry, too many clients already" or "remaining connection slots are reserved", typically during traffic peaks or after scaling out application instances.

chunks.title: PostgreSQL "too many clients already"
chunks.text: Compare current connections with the limit using `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;` and `SHOW max_connections;`. Group by application and state to find idle connections held by pools that are too large. Many sessions in "idle in transaction" indicate application code that opens a transaction and never commits.

chunks.title: PostgreSQL "too many clients already"
chunks.text: Reduce per-instance pool sizes so that instances multiplied by pool size stays below max_connections. Put PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode in front of the database. Terminate stuck sessions with `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` and set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`. Raise max_connections only with matching memory, because each connection reserves its own memory.

chunks.title: PostgreSQL "too many clients already"
chunks.text: Size connection pools deliberately, use a pooler or Amazon RDS Proxy for serverless clients, and alert when connections exceed 80% of the limit.

chunks.title: SSH brute-force login attempts
chunks.text: /var/log/auth.log or `journalctl -u ssh` fills with "Failed password" and "Invalid user" lines from many IP addresses, and CPU rises from sshd handling connections.

chunks.title: SSH brute-force login attempts
chunks.text: Count attempts per source with `grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -n`. Check whether any attempt succeeded by searching for "Accepted" lines from unknown addresses, and review `last` and `lastb`.

chunks.title: SSH brute-force login attempts
chunks.text: Disable password logins by setting `PasswordAuthentication no` and `PermitRootLogin no` in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, then reload sshd. Install fail2ban with an sshd jail to ban addresses after repeated failures. Restrict port 22 in the firewall or cloud security group to known administrative IP ranges. If any login succeeded unexpectedly, treat the host as compromised and rotate keys.

chunks.title: SSH brute-force login attempts
chunks.text: Use key-based authentication only, prefer a bastion host or AWS Systems Manager Session Manager instead of public SSH, and alert on bursts of authentication failures.

chunks.title: SSH "Permission denied (publickey)"
chunks.text: Connecting with `ssh user@host` fails immediately with "Permission denied (publickey)" even though the key was added to the server.

chunks.title: SSH "Permission denied (publickey)"
chunks.text: Run the client with `ssh -vvv` to see which keys are offered and whether the server rejects them. On the server, check `journalctl -u ssh` for "Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes". sshd ignores authorized_keys when the home directory, ~/.ssh or the file is writable by group or others. Confirm the login user is correct; Amazon Linux uses ec2-user and Ubuntu images use ubuntu.

chunks.title: SSH "Permission denied (publickey)"
chunks.text: Fix permissions with `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` and `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, and make sure the user owns both. Pass the right key explicitly with `ssh -i key.pem`. On SELinux systems run `restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh`. For a lost key on EC2, use EC2 Instance Connect or Session Manager to add a new public key.

chunks.title: SSH "Permission denied (publickey)"
chunks.text: Manage authorized keys through configuration management, keep a second access path such as Session Manager, and document the default user for each image.

chunks.title: systemd service fails to start
chunks.text: `systemctl start app` returns an error, the unit shows "failed" or "activating (auto-restart)" in `systemctl status`, and the application is unreachable after a reboot.

chunks.title: systemd service fails to start
chunks.text: Run `systemctl status app` for the last log lines and exit code, then `journalctl -u app -b --no-pager -n 100` for the full output of the current boot. Exit status 203/EXEC means the ExecStart binary is missing or not executable; 217/USER means the configured user does not exist. Check that environment files referenced by `EnvironmentFile=` exist. Validate the unit with `systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/app.service`.

chunks.title: systemd service fails to start
chunks.text: Fix the path, permissions or user in the unit file, then run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` before restarting, because systemd caches unit definitions. If the unit hit its start limit, clear it with `systemctl reset-failed app`. Enable it at boot with `systemctl enable --now app`.

chunks.title: systemd service fails to start
chunks.text: Use `Restart=on-failure` with `RestartSec=` to recover from transient errors, declare dependencies with `After=` and `Wants=network-online.target`, and keep unit files in version control.

chunks.title: System clock drift
chunks.text: TLS handshakes fail with "certificate is not yet valid", AWS API calls return "Signature expired" or "RequestTimeTooSkewed", Kerberos logins fail and log timestamps disagree between hosts.

chunks.title: System clock drift
chunks.text: Check synchronisation with `timedatectl status` and look for "System clock synchronized: yes". With chrony, run `chronyc tracking` for the current offset and `chronyc sources -v` for reachable servers. Confirm outbound UDP port 123 is allowed.

chunks.title: System clock drift
chunks.text: Enable time sync with `sudo timedatectl set-ntp true` and restart chronyd. Step a large offset immediately with `sudo chronyc makestep`. On EC2, use the Amazon Time Sync Service at 169.254.169.123, which needs no internet access.

chunks.title: System clock drift
chunks.text: Run chrony on every host, alert when the offset exceeds 100 ms, and avoid manually setting the clock on servers.

chunks.title: TLS certificate expired or about to expire
chunks.text: Browsers show "Your connection is not private" with NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID, API clients fail with "certificate has expired", and monitoring reports a falling days-to-expiry value.

chunks.title: TLS certificate expired or about to expire
chunks.text: Check the served certificate with `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer`. Confirm the web server is serving the renewed file and not a stale copy. For Let's Encrypt, run `sudo certbot certificates` and inspect the renewal timer with `systemctl list-timers | grep certbot`.

chunks.title: TLS certificate expired or about to expire
chunks.text: Renew with `sudo certbot renew`, then reload nginx or Apache so the new certificate is loaded. If HTTP-01 validation fails, ensure port 80 is reachable and not redirected away from /.well-known/acme-challenge. Install the full chain, not only the leaf certificate, to avoid intermediate errors on some clients.

chunks.title: TLS certificate expired or about to expire
chunks.text: Automate renewal with a timer and a deploy hook that reloads the server, and alert when any certificate has fewer than 21 days remaining. Managed certificates from AWS Certificate Manager renew automatically.

chunks.title: Too many open files
chunks.text: Applications log "Too many open files" or "EMFILE", new connections are refused under load and the error disappears after a restart.

chunks.title: Too many open files
chunks.text: Count descriptors held by the process with `ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l` and compare with its limit in `cat /proc/PID/limits`. Services started by systemd ignore /etc/security/limits.conf and use the unit's `LimitNOFILE=` value. A steadily rising count indicates a descriptor leak, such as sockets or files that are never closed.

chunks.title: Too many open files
chunks.text: Raise the limit for the service by adding `LimitNOFILE=65536` in a drop-in created with `systemctl edit app`, then restart it. For interactive shells, raise it with `ulimit -n`. Fix leaks in code by closing files and sockets, for example with context managers.

chunks.title: Too many open files
chunks.text: Export the open descriptor count as a metric, set explicit limits in unit files and container runtimes, and include connection churn in load tests.
